report:
Short answer: probably yes for some people, but the effect looks modest and is not a substitute for standard care.

The best direct evidence is a 2023 systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized trials in adults with depressive disorder, which concluded magnesium supplementation significantly lowered depression scores while noting prior RCT findings were inconsistent: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2023.1333261/full. An earlier randomized trial in 126 adults with mild-to-moderate depression found 248 mg/day elemental magnesium chloride improved depression and anxiety scores within two weeks and was well tolerated: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0180067. Observational data point the same way: a 2024 dose-response meta-analysis estimated highest vs lowest magnesium intake had ~34% lower depression risk, but diet studies cannot prove causality: https://academic.oup.com/nutritionreviews/article-abstract/83/2/217/7685053.

Mechanisms are plausible—NMDA/glutamate modulation, stress-axis and inflammation effects—but trials are small, short, use different salts/doses, and often don’t assess baseline deficiency. Benefit may be greatest when intake/status is low.

Safety: food magnesium is not the concern; supplements commonly cause diarrhea/cramping, and the adult UL for supplements/medicines is 350 mg/day, with caution in kidney disease and drug interactions: https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Magnesium-HealthProfessional/.
